items.evidence: Table 6 gives these medians and asymmetric intervals. The chart uses the larger uncertainty; independent draws can reverse neighbouring boundaries.
items.source: [Harrigan et al.](https://robintrayler.github.io/publications_files/Harrigan_2021.pdf), full text, especially Table 6; [ICS chart](https://stratigraphy.org/ICSchart/ChronostratChart2024-12.pdf), complete chart.

items.claim: “Do not relabel a stage from a date”; propagate approximately 2 Myr Early Devonian uncertainty through a “joint, ordered age model”.
items.evidence: ICS explicitly distinguishes numerical calibration from stratigraphic definition. Harrigan's ordered age–depth framework supports joint propagation rather than independent boundary perturbations.
items.source: [ICS chart](https://stratigraphy.org/ICSchart/ChronostratChart2024-12.pdf), complete chart; [Harrigan et al.](https://robintrayler.github.io/publications_files/Harrigan_2021.pdf), full text.

items.claim: Reconstructed ocean widths: Iapetus >4,000 km at 487 Ma, 1,200/500 km at 444 Ma; Avalonian rifting about 490 Ma; Rheic >3,500 then about 7,000 km; collision 430–420 Ma.
items.evidence: The numerical reconstruction summaries match the cited accounts. Relabelling them interpretation correctly distinguishes reconstructed geography from direct observations.
items.source: [Cocks and Torsvik 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gr.2020.09.008), indexed full-text passages read; direct opening blocked. [Cocks and Torsvik 2011](https://www.earthdynamics.org/papers-ED/2011/2011-Cocks_Torsvik-ESR.pdf), abstract read.

items.claim: Tropical sea-surface temperatures “32–37 °C”, approximately “5 °C” Hirnantian cooling, and ice volume at or above the Pleistocene maximum.
items.evidence: These match the clumped-isotope reconstruction, although the source qualifies maximum ice volume as likely equal to or greater than the Pleistocene maximum.
items.source: [Finnegan et al.](https://biogeochem.wustl.edu/pdfs/Finnegan_Anticosti_Clumped_Science_2011.pdf), full text.

items.claim: “22,332 carbonate and 4,615 phosphate” analyses; means “42.0 ± 3.1” and “35.6 ± 2.4 °C”; approximately “4–10 °C” above Scotese.
items.evidence: Counts and temperatures match. The difference is an approximate comparison between differently defined reconstructions, appropriately identified as the primer author's calculation.
items.source: [Grossman and Joachimski](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-11493-1.pdf), full text; [Scotese et al.](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/169823/1/Scotese_etal_phan_temp_AAM.pdf), full text.

items.claim: Target variable: “Change in seawater δ18O”; two shifts of approximately “+2‰ over about 1.5 Myr”.
items.evidence: The measured excursions are in conodont phosphate δ18O, not seawater δ18O. Their interpretation involves temperature and potentially seawater composition.
items.source: [Trotter et al.](https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/items/9194eff1-051b-4058-8d66-02970708fce4), repository abstract read; full text inaccessible.

items.claim: Lochkovian low-latitude seawater “about 30 °C”; Middle Devonian “23–25 °C”.
items.evidence: Both values appear in the abstract. They describe reconstructed tropical seawater temperatures, conditional on isotope calibration and assumed seawater composition.
items.source: [Joachimski et al.](https://cris.fau.de/publications/111999844/), abstract read.

items.claim: Scotese: tropics mostly “25–32 °C”; Pragian sea-level fall approximately “100 m”; Early–Middle Devonian global mean “18.7 °C”.
items.evidence: The reconstruction reports these quantities and the Ludlow–Lochkovian warm interval. Tropical temperatures have exceptions, including a colder Hirnantian.
items.source: [Scotese et al.](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/169823/1/Scotese_etal_phan_temp_AAM.pdf), full text.

items.claim: Possible Darriwilian ice onset; “three glacial cycles” under Hirnantian coverage; glacial maximum approximately “0.2 Myr”.
items.evidence: Darriwilian onset is model-dependent; the three cycles span upper Katian–lowermost Silurian. The 0.2 Myr estimate also depends on stratigraphic interpolation.
items.source: [Pohl et al.](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/8057556/8057571), [Ghienne et al.](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/6848045/6853496), and [Ling et al.](https://finneganlab.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/ling-et-al-2019.pdf), full texts.

items.claim: Foster: “1,241 estimates from five proxies”, coverage from “420 Ma”, Devonian “maximum about 2,000 ppm”.
items.evidence: Count, methods and coverage match. Approximately 2,000 ppm describes the reconstructed long-term level, not an upper bound on individual estimates and uncertainties.
items.source: [Foster et al.](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/111546755/ncomms14845.pdf), full text.

items.claim: Witkowski: “460–440 Ma”, approximately “450 rising to 700 µatm”; “about 1,400 µatm in the Devonian”.
items.evidence: Numbers match, but the Devonian observations discussed are around 380–355 Ma, outside this programme's Early Devonian window; temperature assumptions strongly influence estimates.
items.source: [Witkowski et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261654/), full text.

items.claim: Franks: below “1,000 ppm for most of the record”; against prolonged “2,000–3,000 ppm” post-Devonian swings.
items.evidence: This accurately summarises the paper's long-term conclusion. It explicitly allows shorter excursions and describes higher CO2 before approximately 390 Ma.
items.source: [Franks et al.](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/110368/1/Franks%20et%20al%20%282014%29%20%20New%20palaeo-CO2%20model%20GRL.pdf), full text.

items.claim: GEOCLIM atmospheric CO2: approximately “5,600 falling to 2,800 ppmv by the Llandovery”, then rising in the Early Devonian.
items.evidence: The primary abstract reports more than 20 PAL in the Furongian, approximately 10 PAL in the Llandovery, and subsequent Early Devonian increase.
items.source: [Nardin et al.](https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsa/gsabulletin/article-abstract/123/5-6/1181/125670/Modeling-the-early-Paleozoic-long-term-climatic?redirectedFrom=fulltext), indexed publisher abstract read; full text inaccessible.

items.claim: At 445 Ma: 8 PAL CO2, approximately 2,200 ppm using 278 ppm/PAL; 0.6 PAL O2, approximately 14%; NPP 18.7 versus 10.5 GtC yr−1, approximately 30% versus 17%; C:P approximately 2,000 versus 100, range 800–4,300; P weathering 24-fold, range 15–43.
items.evidence: Gas assumptions, productivity and C:P values match. The 24-fold phosphorus effect specifically concerns moss on granite; liverwort experiments yielded different amplification.
items.source: [Lenton et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5024600/), full text, including embedded supplementary figures and tables.

items.claim: HadCM3L scotese_02 uses prescribed CO2, extended before 420 Ma, with “1,093–2,513 ppm” across the window.
items.evidence: Input status is correct. Those extrema belong to 485–385 Ma slices; listed 455–395 Ma slices span approximately 1,297–2,102 ppm.
items.source: [Valdes et al.](https://cp.copernicus.org/articles/17/1483/2021/), full text; [Zenodo dataset](https://zenodo.org/records/8237751), metadata read; local hadcm3l_experiment_info.csv checked.

items.claim: Homerian charcoal at Pen-y-lan predates basal Pridoli charcoal; both newly discussed assemblages are dominated by nematophytes.
items.evidence: The charcoal paper identifies Homerian and Ludlow assemblages dominated by nematophytes. BGS independently assigns the Pen-y-lan succession to the Homerian.
items.source: [Glasspool and Gastaldo 2022](https://web.colby.edu/ragastal/files/2023/07/2022_Glasspool_Gastaldo_GEOLOGY_WIldfire.pdf), full text; [BGS account](https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Wenlock_Series,_Silurian,_Wales), relevant section read.

items.claim: Fire thresholds: 13–35%; 15–17% at 420–400 Ma; approximately 15% for smouldering, 19% for probable combustion; 16%, approximately 0.75 PAL; substantially uninterrupted Devonian fire.
items.evidence: These accurately report differing published interpretations. Thresholds depend on experimental conditions; uninterrupted oxygen above 16% remains Glasspool and Gastaldo's inference.
items.source: [Scott and Glasspool](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16832054/), abstract; [Lenton et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5024600/), full text; [Krause et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6172248/), indexed full text; [Glasspool and Gastaldo 2022](https://web.colby.edu/ragastal/files/2023/07/2022_Glasspool_Gastaldo_GEOLOGY_WIldfire.pdf), full text; [2024 paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/383474031_Don't_mind_the_charcoal_gap_A_reassessment_of_Devonian_wildfire), publicly available article text.

items.claim: Horneophyton: “In either reading ... the corm lacks conducting cells.”
items.section: Horneophyton card: conducting_tissue, Morphology and anatomy, Model transfer
items.evidence: Kenrick and Long explicitly describe conducting cells in the rhizome centre and edge, continuous with the aerial conducting core.
items.source: [Kenrick and Long](https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.70850), full text, Results and Discussion.

items.claim: Horneophyton modelling examples retain “39 to 49 µm spores” and stature “up to about 20 cm”.
items.section: Horneophyton card: Why it matters for modelling
items.evidence: Eggert reports the spore range; Kenrick and Long describe stature below 20 cm. Neither supplies measured hydraulic performance or a meiotic-error rate.
items.source: [Eggert](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2441808), indexed primary abstract read; [Kenrick and Long](https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.70850), full text.

items.claim: “Microphyllous lycophytes outside the crown”: Asteroxylon and Baragwanathia; lycophyte crown clock estimate “431–411 Ma”.
items.evidence: The stem/crown distinction and clock interval are appropriate. Asteroxylon's appendages lack internal vascularisation, so calling both taxa microphyllous needs qualification.
items.source: [Hetherington et al.](https://elifesciences.org/articles/69447), full text; [Harris et al.](https://bpb-eu-w2.wpmucdn.com/blogs.bristol.ac.uk/dist/3/589/files/2022/09/Harris_et_al_2022.pdf), full text; [Kerp](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5745331/), indexed full-text passages read.

items.claim: “Eophytes have never been placed by a cladistic analysis.”
items.evidence: Hooper makes that statement, but Clark includes eophytes and describes Bayesian morphological inference with unconstrained fossil placement. The apparent conflict needs reconciliation.
items.source: [Hooper et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-026-02432-3), full text; [Clark et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-023-01513-x), full text, especially Methods.

items.claim: Hooper: 27 characters, 27 living and 11 fossil genera, four methods, three timetrees; bounds 459.1–426.9 and 431.2–420.7 Ma; 55 Myr younger; gap as little as 19 Myr.
items.evidence: Counts, bounds and 55 Myr shift match. Minima also have soft tails; unenveloped ancestry is model-dependent. The 19 Myr gap needs its fossil benchmark.
items.source: [Hooper et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-026-02432-3), full text; supplementary calibration tables not examined.

items.claim: Separate crown-embryophyte results: Morris 515.2–473.5 Ma, Harris 515–493 Ma, Hooper 457–450 Ma, Su 980–682 Ma; Harris relaxed-maxima result 597–540 Ma.
items.evidence: These reported intervals match their respective analyses. Su's ancient interval specifically uses Strategy 2; the revised separation avoids constructing a pooled uncertainty interval.
items.source: [Morris et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5877938/), [Harris et al.](https://bpb-eu-w2.wpmucdn.com/blogs.bristol.ac.uk/dist/3/589/files/2022/09/Harris_et_al_2022.pdf), [Hooper et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-026-02432-3), and [Su et al.](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/770f/eefa7462e68d090c0af2867d9616919c25fb.pdf), full texts.

items.claim: An ancestral trilete spore permits secondary cryptospory; a character's fossil first occurrence supplies a crown maximum only under preservation and sampling assumptions.
items.evidence: These are sound logical qualifications, not demonstrated historical events. An inferred ancestral state does not establish irreversible character evolution or immediate fossil detection.
items.source: [Hooper et al.](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-026-02432-3), full text; assessment of the inference made from its reconstruction and calibrations.

items.claim: “Origination and extinction times before the first fossil ... can be estimated from a preservation and sampling model, or from clock calibrations.”
items.evidence: Origination can precede first occurrence; extinction of the same sampled lineage cannot. Extinction beyond last occurrence requires appropriate fossil-process modelling, not ordinary divergence clocks.
items.source: [Silvestro et al.](https://doi.org/10.1093/sysbio/syu006), primary abstract read; [Morris et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5877938/), full text.

omissions: Harrigan includes the Parry Rhynie date among its numerical inputs. Testing Rhynie against those calibrated boundaries therefore requires dependence between the fossil-date evidence and boundary model, beyond merely ordering boundary draws. [Harrigan et al., Table 4](https://robintrayler.github.io/publications_files/Harrigan_2021.pdf).

Kenrick and Long document conducting tissue within the corm/rhizome and interpret the H-type system primarily as solute-conducting, with no clear specialised water-conducting cells. The card's “probably for solute transport as well as water” transfers their broader ancestral-system hypothesis too directly to Horneophyton. [Full text](https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.70850).

Hooper explicitly doubts whether the Dalby specimens' trilete marks are compression artefacts. Its calibration distributions also allocate 2.5% probability beyond each endpoint; identifying only the maximum as soft incompletely describes implementation. [Full text](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-026-02432-3).

Su also obtains 518–500 Ma with the restrictive calibration strategy and 919–639 Ma without those maximum bounds. Including these alongside its 980–682 Ma result would show within-study calibration sensitivity. [Full text](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/770f/eefa7462e68d090c0af2867d9616919c25fb.pdf).

Witkowski's Devonian observations discussed in the article fall around 380–355 Ma. Its Ordovician CO2 conversion uses approximately 10 °C seawater, and the authors attribute part of the reconstructed CO2 shift to temperature assumptions; the CO2 and temperature evidence are consequently dependent. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261654/).

Lenton's sensitivity table gives ice-free productivity of 7.8, 18.7 and 27.1 GtC yr−1 at 4, 8 and 16 PAL CO2 with O2 fixed at 0.6 PAL. Thus “depends on the ice scenario as much as on the plants” is not an established sensitivity ranking. [Table S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5024600/).

The 24-fold phosphorus-weathering amplification concerns Physcomitrella on granite; Marchantia experiments give 9–13-fold phosphorus amplification on basalt. Porada's approximately 3× compares global weathering with today's global flux, rather than measuring the same experimental enhancement factor. [Lenton](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5024600/), [Porada](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms12113.pdf).

Grossman and Joachimski's full compilation counts differ from the screened data used in reconstruction: 11,893 carbonate and 4,427 phosphate analyses. Its temperatures assume hydrosphere isotope behaviour and apply ice-volume and latitude corrections. [Full text](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-11493-1.pdf).

Ghienne's three cycles extend from upper Katian into lowermost Silurian and are explicitly presented as a stratigraphic interpretation. Combining them under a single Hirnantian coverage label loses this distinction. [Full text](https://backoffice.biblio.ugent.be/download/6848045/6853496).

Cascales-Miñana and colleagues document considerable spore variation within Horneophyton sporangia and a possible dyad produced by tetrad breakage. Abnormal fossil groupings should therefore not automatically become biological meiotic errors in a model. [Full text](https://orbi.uliege.be/bitstream/2268/259106/1/1-s2.0-S0034666721001676-main%282%29.pdf).

Clark's methodological account creates an apparent conflict with the categorical statement that eophytes have never undergone cladistic analysis. Resolve the taxon and analysis scope before repeating that historical claim as settled. [Full text](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41477-023-01513-x).
overall: The revision substantially improves the primer's treatment of calibration, competing clocks, environmental evidence and identifiability, but it is not yet a dependable modelling reference. Consequential remaining problems include the Horneophyton corm contradiction, the mislabelled isotope variable, incomplete temporal coverage statements and inconsistent handling of uncertainty between primer and card; section 6 was excluded.

review_points.point: 1. Stratigraphic assignments, numerical evidence and joint boundary uncertainty
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: The primer's rules are substantially corrected. The card still labels numerical dates as Pragian/“earliest Emsian”, and the boundary proposal does not discuss dependence on Rhynie dates already used by Harrigan.

review_points.point: 2. Living backbone, stem lycophytes and alternative fossil placements
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: The diagram removes the false extinct-grade sequence and crown assignment. Some fossil memberships remain categorical, Asteroxylon is called microphyllous, and the “never analysed” eophyte statement needs reconciliation with Clark.

review_points.point: 3. Divergence clocks, soft maxima, secondary cryptospory and separate estimates
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: The central corrections are present. Hooper's ancestral morphology is initially stated categorically before its model dependence appears; Dalby identification uncertainty and soft minimum implementation remain insufficiently explicit.

review_points.point: 4. Horneophyton anatomy, earlier charcoal and the Devonian charcoal gap
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: Both anatomical interpretations and newer charcoal studies are included. The card nevertheless denies corm conducting cells despite the new source and overstates evidence for combined water and solute transport.

review_points.point: 5. Environmental evidence, model outputs, assumed inputs and plant temperatures
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: The tables and sensitivity-scenario wording are major improvements. Remaining losses include conodont versus seawater δ18O, late Devonian evidence presented under window coverage, broad climate-suite extrema and unqualified claims about proxy absence.

review_points.point: 6. Identifiability, recovery tests, calibration circularity and ghost lineages
review_points.where_uncertainty_is_still_lost: Recovery tests and circularity are explicit, but “tractable” still denotes execution feasibility. Testing maxima against fossils already used in calibration also needs independence safeguards; the ghost-lineage sentence incorrectly places extinction before first occurrence.
The erroneous “Ediacaran, not Neoproterozoic” contrast is removed. The replacement correctly reports Harris's 597–540 Ma sensitivity result without treating those nested time units as alternatives.
